title: Packaging Sass for Reuse
learning_outcomes: Explain packaging sass for reuse and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply packaging sass for reuse in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **Packaging Sass for Reuse** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect preparing a reusable sass package with organizing public entrypoints, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: Treat the toolchain as a repeatable pipeline: keep editable SCSS as input, let Dart Sass compile an explicit entrypoint, and inspect the generated CSS or map. Separate local setup problems from errors in the stylesheet itself.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: A reliable workflow gives every teammate the same command and an observable output. Commit source and scripts; decide deliberately whether generated CSS and source maps belong in the repository or are build artifacts.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Packaging Sass for Reuse
content_blocks.code:
library/
  _index.scss      # documented public entrypoint
  _tokens.scss     # defaults and configuration
  _mixins.scss     # public reusable patterns
  _internal.scss   # private helpers
content_blocks.expected_output: A consumer can load the documented entrypoint with @use and depend on the published public API.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Use the command or build configuration shown for packaging sass for reuse in a tiny local project. Record the command you ran, the file it created or diagnostic it produced, and one way you verified the result.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
